title: Capstone B: a breach across teams
summary: A breach at a payroll company that crosses every team: a password spray on the VPN, a scan and a script with secrets on a file share, a hop to an application server, salary files copied out on-premises and from the cloud. No hints. Rebuild it, scope it, contain it, file and notify on time as a data processor, leave new detections behind, and brief the board.
tools: Everything: Linux, Event viewer, Merged timeline, SIEM search, Sigma rules, Cloud IAM simulator, CERT-In filing, Report builder
handin: An executive briefing, a technical report, a notification pack and a new detection.
rubric: Entry, movement and theft reconstructed across VPN, network, Windows and cloud, with times
Scope: which data, whose, and how many people, with the counts shown
Containment and fixes in the right order; the cloud policy at 0 attacker actions and 0 broken
CERT-In filed on time, and the notification order right for a processor and its clients
New detections tested on the evidence
Executive briefing a board can decide from
Technical report complete and consistent with the timeline

script.intro: Hello, and welcome to Capstone B: a breach across teams. This is the last seminar in the series, and it has no hints. Indigo Ledger is a payroll company in Pune. It runs payroll for other companies, so the data at risk isn't really Indigo's. It belongs to its clients' employees: their names, salaries, bank accounts and PAN numbers. On Monday the twenty-ninth of November 2027, a cloud alert fires about a payroll bucket. The trail behind it runs through the VPN, the office network, a Windows application server and the cloud account. Your job is all of it: rebuild what happened, scope it, contain it, file and notify on time, leave detections behind, and brief the board. This is an exercise. It's set after India's DPDP breach duties begin on the thirteenth of May 2027, so before any real incident, check the current text of every rule. This lab follows its own summary of each one. The CERT-In six-hour reporting window is older and settled: it comes from the 2022 directions. One note on time. Every time in this case is UTC. Pune is five and a half hours ahead, so the alert at 05:20 in the logs is 10:50 on the office clock. Work like a team of one, and let's begin.

steps.say: Step one: brief, custody, plan. With no hints, the order you work in is the only guide you have. So before you open a single log, do three things. Read the README and the alert. Hash every file, so you can prove later that nothing changed after you received it. And write a short plan. The Linux cell lists every file, prints a SHA-256 hash for each, and then prints the cloud egress alert.
steps.after: Twelve files, counting the README and the CERT-In form file, each with its hash. Save that list; it's your chain of custody. Now the alert. At 05:20, cloud monitoring saw 12 objects, 612 megabytes, read from the payroll-exports bucket by payroll-backup, from 198.51.100.150, between 04:22 and 04:24. And the line that makes it suspicious: payroll-backup normally only uploads, from the office address 203.0.113.88. D. Kapoor, the SOC on-call, acknowledged it at 05:35, and the incident was declared at 05:41. The lab starts the clock at 05:35, when a person noticed. Six hours from then is 11:35. If someone argues for the alert time, 05:20, plan to the earlier one; a filing at 09:10 would beat both. Your plan: entry first, then the network, the server and the cloud, but scope early, because the clocks need facts. Answer the questions: 12, and 05:35.

steps.say: Step two: how they got in. The alert came from the cloud, but the cloud key had to come from somewhere. Start at the front door, the VPN. The cell counts every VPN line from the alert's address, 198.51.100.150, shows the ones that succeeded, and then looks up the intern account in the directory export.
steps.after: Eighteen lines from that address, one per account, from 02:51:04 to 02:59:42, about half a minute apart. That's a password spray: one common password tried against many accounts, slowly, so no single account locks out. Seventeen fail with bad_password. Those accounts all have MFA, so even a right guess would still have needed a second factor. One succeeds: at 02:58:39, intern.payroll, MFA not enrolled, given the VPN address 10.80.9.33. Notice the spray carries on after the success, to q.verma and r.ghosh. That's a script, not a person typing. Compare a normal login: a.menon at 02:40, from 49.36.200.225, with MFA. Now the directory. intern.payroll is a former intern. Their leaving date was the thirty-first of July 2027, four months ago, yet the account is still active, has no MFA, and is in VPN-Users and IT-Scripts-Read. It should have been disabled on the last day. Answer the questions: 18, and intern.payroll.

steps.say: Step three: across the network. Once inside, an attacker needs to know what's there. Zeek watches the office network. conn.log records every connection, and smb_files.log records files opened on Windows shares. The cell takes every connection from 10.80.9.33 to port 445, the Windows file sharing port, counts the different addresses by how the connection ended, then prints the file actions.
steps.after: 37 connections ended REJ, refused, and 7 ended SF, a normal finish. That's 44 different addresses. From 03:15:03 it walks 10.80.2.1 to 10.80.2.40, one every three seconds, then four servers, finishing at 03:17:40. Three addresses in the 10.80.2 range answered, plus all four servers, including files01 at 10.80.1.15 and pay-app01 at 10.80.1.40. A sweep like this is loud, and nobody normal needs to touch forty addresses' file shares in two minutes. Then the file log. At 03:40:20 it opens scripts backslash backup-config.ps1 on the IT dollar share of files01. That's why IT-Scripts-Read mattered. The captured copy shows what's inside: the local administrator password used on every app server, and the cloud backup key, SCKA9F2LQ7MX4TB1, with its secret. One file, two doors. At 04:12:40, a write: t.ps1 into Users backslash Public on pay-app01. Answer the questions: 44, and backup-config.ps1.

steps.say: Step four: on the application server. pay-app01 runs the payroll application, and its exports sit in the exports folder on the D drive.The Event viewer opens its Security log, filtered to localadmin. Four event IDs matter: 4624, a logon; 4672, special privileges; 4688, a new process; and 1102, the audit log was cleared.
steps.after: Seven events. At 04:05:09, a 4624: localadmin, domain PAY-APP01, logon type 3, over the network, with NTLM, from 10.80.9.33, the intern's VPN address. Domain PAY-APP01 means a local account on the server itself, so the password from the script worked. A 4672 follows with debug, backup and take-ownership privileges. Compare normal: svc-backup at 01:00 with logon type 5, a service, and c.iyer at 02:44 over Kerberos from 10.80.2.14. Then the processes. At 04:13:02, PowerShell runs t.ps1 with the execution policy bypassed. At 04:31:40, Compress-Archive zips every CSV in that exports folder into e.zip. At 04:52:28, curl uploads e.zip to upload.drop-files.example. At 05:01:03 both files are deleted, and at 05:02:00 the log is cleared. But Zeek saw the upload: at 04:52:30, pay-app01 sends about 182 megabytes to 203.0.113.230 on port 443, over five minutes. One more lesson: this copy still holds the events before the clear. In real life you usually only have those if they were forwarded off the server first. Answer the questions: upload.drop-files.example, and 1102.

steps.say: Step five: in the cloud. The second door was the backup key. The cloud audit trail records every call: who, which key, from where, what action, on what, and whether it worked. The cell counts the GetObject lines, the downloads, then counts lines by client folder in the bucket.
steps.after: Twelve downloads. The folder counts show three each for Coral Small Finance Bank, Fjord Design India and Pine Textiles, but six for Lotus Motors. That's the trap. Three of the Lotus lines are normal: the nightly upload at 01:30 from 203.0.113.88, a PutObject, with the user agent indigo-backup. So it's three downloads per client. The attacker's calls come from 198.51.100.150, the spray address, with a different tool. At 04:20:03, GetCallerIdentity, which means who am I. At 04:20:40, list the bucket. From 04:22:00 to 04:24:01, twelve downloads: September, October and November 2027 for four clients. At 04:30:10, PutBucketPolicy, an attempt to change the bucket's access, is denied. Not because anyone planned it, but because the key's policy simply didn't list that action. It already allowed get, list, put and delete on everything. Lucky, not designed. At 05:40, c.iyer logs in to the console with MFA: that's the response starting. Answer the question: 12.

steps.say: Step six: one timeline. Four sources, one clock. The merged timeline reads the VPN log, the server's Security log and the cloud audit trail together, sorted by time. All three are in UTC, so they line up directly. Star the key events and download the timeline for the report.
steps.after: Six starred events tell the story. 02:58:39, the intern's account gets in. 04:05:09, localadmin logs on to pay-app01. 04:20:03, the cloud key asks who am I. 04:31:40, the exports are zipped. 04:52:28, the upload. 05:02:00, the log is cleared. Around them, from the other files: the scan at 03:15, the script read at 03:40, the alert at 05:20, someone looking at 05:35, and the VPN session closed by an admin at 06:02:10. Two routes out for the same data: the cloud downloads and the upload from the server. And the gap: the last cloud download was at 04:24, and nobody looked for over an hour. From the VPN login at 02:58:39 to the first download at 04:22:00 is 83 minutes and 21 seconds. Answer the question: 83.

steps.say: Step seven: scope. Whose data, and how much. Every clock and every notice depends on these numbers, so show your working. clients.csv lists each client, how many of its employees are in the exports, whether it's regulated by the RBI, and where the employees are. The cell prints it and adds up the people.
steps.after: Lotus Motors, 1,240. Pine Textiles, 860. Coral Small Finance Bank, 310, and it's RBI-regulated. Fjord Design India, 95, with an EU parent and 12 EU staff on secondment. Total: 2,505 people. Count people, not files; each person appears in more than one month. The data is names, salaries, bank accounts and PAN: enough for fraud. Now the key point of this case. Indigo is the data processor. The clients decide why and how the data is used, so they are the data fiduciaries. In this lab's summary, the fiduciaries tell the Data Protection Board and their own employees, and Indigo must tell them at once and give them the facts. Coral is a bank with its own six-hour clock that starts when it learns, so Coral needs facts from Indigo fast. Fjord's EU staff may bring in GDPR, and that's for the parent to decide. Answer the question: 2,505.

steps.say: Step eight: contain and fix. Order matters. Cut off access before you clean up, keep the evidence, then fix the causes. For the cloud, the Cloud IAM simulator replays every recorded call against a new policy. The draft shrinks the backup key to one action, PutObject, into payroll-exports, only from the office address 203.0.113.88. And it adds a guardrail: reading client data from that bucket needs MFA.
steps.after: The replay: 0 attacker actions allowed, and 0 normal actions broken. The nightly upload at 01:30 still works, and every one of the attacker's calls fails, because they came from the wrong address and asked for things the key no longer has. c.iyer's admin access isn't touched, and it uses MFA anyway. Now the order. First, cut the VPN session, disable intern.payroll, and block 198.51.100.150 and 203.0.113.230. Second, revoke the backup key and reset localadmin on every server, with a different password on each, which is what LAPS manages. Third, isolate pay-app01 and keep its disk image. Isolate, don't wipe: the image is evidence. Then the causes: take secrets out of the IT scripts and restrict the share, MFA on every VPN account, accounts disabled on leaving day, and the least-privilege key. Answer the question: 0.

steps.say: Step nine: file and notify. The CERT-In filing tool takes the form, checks it, and then delivers messages to your inbox as time passes. Remember who's who: Indigo is the processor, and its four clients are the fiduciaries.
steps.after: The form: occurred at 02:58, detected at 05:35, filed at 09:10. That's three hours and thirty-five minutes after noticing, well inside the deadline of 11:35. Type, data breach. The checks want four things: the indicator 198.51.100.150, how they got in through the VPN account, which cloud storage was read, and what you've done so far. Two messages arrive. Coral's CISO: we're RBI-regulated, our staff payroll is with you, we need facts within the hour for our own six-hour duty. And CERT-In: preserve VPN, server and cloud logs for 180 days, and share the indicators in STIX or CSV. Now the order. CERT-In, by 11:35. Every client at once, by 07:00, with Coral first. The clients notify the Data Protection Board and their employees without delay, and Indigo supplies the facts and a draft notice. Fjord's EU parent today, for its GDPR decision on 72 hours. The insurer today. Answer the question: clients.

steps.say: Step ten: leave detections behind. Every incident should leave the organisation better at spotting the next one. Two rules. First, a SIEM search for VPN failures, counted by source address. Second, a Sigma rule for a local administrator logging on over the network: event 4624, logon type 3, user localadmin.
steps.after: The search returns one row: 198.51.100.150, 17 failures. In real use you'd alert on one source failing against many different accounts in a short window. The spray ran from 02:51:04 to 02:59:42, so this alert could have fired before 03:00, over two and a half hours before anyone noticed. The Sigma rule matches one event, the attacker's logon at 04:05:09. It doesn't match svc-backup's service logon or c.iyer's Kerberos logon, which is what you want: nothing normal. A local admin account should almost never log on across the network, and with a unique password on each server it's much harder to reuse. The rule lists one false positive: break-glass use in an outage, which should be in the change log. That alert would have fired at 04:05, before any data left. Answer the question: 17.

steps.say: Step eleven: brief the board, report to the team. Two readers, two documents. The board needs to decide, so the one-page note puts the decisions first. The team needs every detail, so the technical report carries the timeline, scope, root cause, actions and indicators. The Report builder has a template for each.
steps.after: The board note opens with the ask: approve today telling all four clients now, MFA on every remote login and same-day removal of leavers this week, and an outside firm to confirm scope. Then severity, critical, and why, in plain words. What we know. And what we don't: who did it, and whether the data has been published or sold. Saying what you don't know is what makes the rest believable. The technical report gives the full timeline, the scope with what wasn't seen, and the root cause: a leaver's account left open without MFA, secrets in a script on a readable share, one local admin password everywhere, and a key that could read everything. It also gives who was told and when: Coral at 06:40, the other clients by 07:00, the insurer at 08:00, and CERT-In at 09:10. Before you finish, check every time in both documents against your downloaded timeline.

steps.say: Step twelve: hand in. The notebook carries every answer, tool result and report from the steps above. Check the list: every file hashed, the timeline starred and downloaded, the cloud policy at 0 and 0, CERT-In filed with no problems, both detections tested, and both documents written. Then press Hand in.
steps.after: The rubric is on screen, thirty points. The most, six, go to rebuilding entry, movement and theft across the VPN, the network, Windows and the cloud, with times. Next, five points for filing CERT-In on time and getting the notification order right for a processor and its clients. Your teacher grades the notebook against this rubric, and your Capstone B certificate is issued once it's graded.

script.outro: That's a breach across every team, handled by one person. A sprayed password on an account that should have been closed, a network sweep, a script holding two secrets, a reused local admin password, and salary files out by two routes. You rebuilt it on one clock, counted 2,505 people, contained it in order, proved the cloud fix at zero and zero, filed inside six hours, put the clients first as the fiduciaries, left two detections behind, and wrote a board note that asks for decisions. This was the final capstone of thirteen seminars. You started with Evidence, notes and handoffs. Then Reading evidence: packets, Linux, Windows and network sensors. Log search and detection as code. SOC triage. Capstone A, the night shift. Incident response. Breach clocks. Identity from both sides. Cloud and DevSecOps. Authorised testing. Design, risk and audit. AI security. And today, Capstone B. Hand in your notebook. Once your teacher has graded it, you'll get a certificate with the hours and a verification number. Many certification bodies let you self-report those hours as CPE; whether they accept them is their decision. Thank you for watching.
